key_terms.meaning: Resistance of a fluid to shear flow; dynamic viscosity μ = shear stress ÷ velocity gradient, in Pa·s (N·s/m²), and kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s or cSt.
A number showing how little an oil's viscosity changes with temperature; high VI means a flatter viscosity–temperature curve and steadier oil films.
The lowest temperature at which an oil gives off enough vapour to flash when a flame is passed over it; the fire-safety limit of the lubricant.
A semi-solid lubricant made of oil held in a soap or other thickener, used where oil cannot be retained or replenished often.
A sliding bearing in which a round shaft (the journal) turns inside a curved bush, carrying load through a fluid film.
A soft tin- or lead-based white-metal bearing alloy with low friction and good embeddability, poured as a thin lining on a steel bush.
The film is thinner than the surface roughness, so load is carried by a very thin film plus surface layers of lubricant; wear occurs but slowly.
A complete fluid film, thick enough to keep the surfaces fully apart, carries the load by pressure generated by the moving surface itself; no metal contact.
A rolling contact bearing using hardened steel balls as rolling elements; low friction, mainly radial and moderate axial load.
A rolling bearing with cylindrical rollers in line contact; high radial capacity, but no axial load capacity.
A roller bearing whose rollers are long and thin (diameter small compared with length); used where radial space is limited.
Partly boundary and partly hydrodynamic; a few high spots touch while other areas are supported on fluid.
ε = e/c, the shaft centre offset e divided by radial clearance c; h₀ = c(1 − ε) is the minimum film thickness.
The thinnest oil gap in a loaded journal bearing; the design must keep it larger than the combined surface roughness.
S = (r/c)² × (μN/P), with r journal radius, c radial clearance, μ viscosity in Pa·s, N speed in rev/s, P = W/(L·d) projected bearing pressure in Pa.
Ratio of bearing length to journal diameter; low values leak oil at the ends, high values run hotter and misalign more.
The constant radial load at which 90% of a group of bearings reaches 1 million revolutions; the load capacity used in life calculation.
The static load that leaves a permanent deformation of 0.0001 × rolling-element diameter at the most heavily loaded contact; the load capacity for non-rotating or very slow bearings.
P = X·F_r + Y·F_a, with F_r radial load, F_a axial load, X and Y load factors from the bearing catalogue; it converts combined loading to one radial-equivalent value.
The life in revolutions (or hours) that 90% of identical bearings reach or exceed under a given load; L10 = (C/P)^p × 10⁶ revolutions, p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings.

takeaways: A lubricant does its job only if it stays between the surfaces, and viscosity is the property that decides whether it can.
Viscosity falls as oil gets hotter, so a lubrication design has to be checked at the running temperature, not the cold start.
Sliding bearings are quiet and cheap but need a full oil film; rolling bearings have low starting friction and need almost no attention.
In a journal bearing the shaft's own rotation drags oil into a wedge, and that converging gap is what builds the pressure that carries the load.
The Sommerfeld number collapses speed, viscosity, clearance and load into one number, which is why a single family of charts serves many bearings.
Raimondi and Boyd charts turn S and L/D into eccentricity, film thickness, friction, oil flow and temperature rise — the five numbers a bearing design needs.
Bearing life falls steeply with load: life goes as (C/P)³ for ball bearings, so a 25% overload can halve or worse the life.
Bearing selection is a loop: guess a bearing, compute P, get required C, pick from the catalogue, then recheck C₀, speed limit and temperature.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move through the full chain — oil choice given the temperature, Sommerfeld number, Raimondi and Boyd chart reading, film thickness and temperature rise, or load rating and L10 life up to a catalogue selection with a static check.

bank.q: Define viscosity and viscosity index. Explain why the same oil may be right for a machine in a Chennai summer and wrong in a cold hill station, and what the designer does about it.
outline: Viscosity definition with μ = τ ÷ (du/dy), units Pa·s; kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ
Viscosity–temperature curve: viscosity drops sharply on heating, rises on cooling
Viscosity index as a measure of flatness of that curve; high VI preferred
Hot running temperature fixes the minimum viscosity that keeps h₀ large enough
Cold start fixes the maximum viscosity that still allows oil to reach the bearing
Practical answers: multigrade oil, high-VI oil, warm-up, oil cooler, thermostat

bank.q: Compare sliding contact and rolling contact bearings under load capacity, friction, starting torque, space, noise, cost and maintenance. Place boundary, mixed and hydrodynamic lubrication on the same picture.
outline: Construction: journal and bush versus inner ring, outer ring and rolling elements
Friction: sliding bearings have higher starting friction; rolling bearings have low starting torque
Load capacity per unit size; shock capacity; damping and noise
Radial space: rolling bearings need more radial depth, needle rollers less
Lubrication regimes: boundary at low speed or high load, mixed in between, hydrodynamic at speed
Where each is used: journal bearing in engines and turbines, rolling bearing in electric motors, fans, gearboxes

bank.q: Explain how a hydrodynamic oil film is generated in a journal bearing. Define eccentricity ratio, minimum film thickness and attitude angle, and state the condition for full film lubrication.
outline: Shaft rotates and drags oil into the converging wedge; oil is incompressible
Pressure rises in the converging region and falls in the diverging region; the resultant balances the load
Equilibrium position: shaft centre offset by e in the direction of rotation
Eccentricity ratio ε = e/c, h₀ = c(1 − ε), attitude angle between load line and line of centres
Full film condition: h₀ well above the combined surface roughness; otherwise boundary or mixed
Requires continuous supply of oil and enough speed and viscosity

bank.q: Define basic dynamic load rating C and basic static load rating C₀ of a rolling bearing. Explain the physical meaning of each and when each governs the selection.
outline: C: load giving 1 million revolutions L10 life, for a rotating bearing
C₀: load causing permanent deformation of 0.0001 times the element diameter at the most loaded contact
C₀ governs for static or very slow, heavily loaded bearings, and for shock loads
C governs for normal rotating service through the life equation
Both are catalogue values for the specific bearing number
Check that the chosen C and C₀ are both adequate, and also check the speed limit

bank.q: A journal of 60 mm diameter and 60 mm length runs at 1200 rpm with SAE 30 oil of μ = 0.020 Pa·s at the working temperature. Radial clearance is 0.06 mm and the load is 6 kN. Compute the Sommerfeld number and the projected bearing pressure.
outline: S ≈ 0.060; state that S is dimensionless and check it lies inside the chart range

bank.q: For a journal bearing with L/D = 1 and Sommerfeld number 0.12, use the Raimondi and Boyd charts to obtain the eccentricity ratio, minimum film thickness, friction variable and oil flow, given c = 0.05 mm, d = 50 mm, N = 1500 rpm. Explain each chart reading.
outline: Enter the ε chart at S = 0.12 for L/D = 1, read ε and h₀ = c(1 − ε)
Enter the friction variable chart (r/c)f versus S, obtain f, then friction torque T = f·W·r
Enter the flow variable chart, obtain Q/(r·c·N·L), then Q in m³/s
Read the temperature-rise chart or use the heat balance ΔT = friction power ÷ (ρ·C_p·Q)
Check h₀ against the surface roughness for full film
State the interpolation and the fact that charts are for finite-length bearings and given boundary conditions

bank.q: A deep groove ball bearing carries a radial load of 5 kN at 900 rpm and must last 10 000 hours. Find the required basic dynamic load rating. Take p = 3.
outline: Revolutions in the life: L = 60 × N × h = 60 × 900 × 10000 = 5.4 × 10⁸ rev
In million revolutions: L10 = 540
Choose the next catalogue bearing with C ≥ 40.7 kN
Check C₀ and the limiting speed for that bearing

bank.q: A bearing carries F_r = 4 kN and F_a = 1.6 kN. From the catalogue X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5, and the application factor is 1.3. Compute the equivalent dynamic load and select the life at 1200 rpm for a bearing with C = 35 kN.
outline: Apply the service factor: P = 1.3 × 4640 ≈ 6032 N
L10 = (C/P)³ = (35000/6032)³ ≈ 195 million revolutions
Comment that increasing C or reducing load raises life steeply

bank.q: Explain why the Sommerfeld number alone does not fix a journal bearing design, and how temperature rise, oil supply and L/D ratio are handled in the design loop.
outline: S depends on μ, which depends on the oil temperature that the bearing itself creates
Friction power heats the oil; viscosity falls; S falls; the operating point moves
Iterative loop: assume a temperature, get μ, compute S, read charts, compute friction and flow, compute ΔT, check the assumed temperature
Side leakage at the ends reduces pressure for small L/D; Raimondi and Boyd curves are given separately for each L/D
Large L/D raises load capacity but also raises temperature and misalignment sensitivity
Convergence check and the final safe value of h₀

bank.q: A newly installed rolling bearing on a pump fails in three months instead of the expected three years. List the likely causes and explain how each one is detected and corrected.
outline: Overload or underestimated P from axial load, unbalance or belt pull
Wrong or insufficient lubricant, or grease loss; check colour,quantity, operating temperature
Contamination: water, dust, grit; check seals and breathing
Misalignment or shaft deflection causing edge loading
Incorrect fits: too tight removes internal clearance, too loose allows creep and fretting
Improper mounting damage, false brinelling during idle vibration
Diagnosis from the failure pattern on raceways plus vibration and temperature records
Corrections: reselect with the real P, better seals, alignment check, correct fits

bank.q: Compare a hydrodynamic journal bearing and a deep groove ball bearing for the two ends of a 7.5 kW, 1440 rpm induction motor. Give the calculation steps you would use for each and justify the choice.
outline: Load estimate for the motor shaft end; both radial and some axial
Rolling bearing route: P, life in hours, required C, catalogue selection, C₀ and speed check
Journal bearing route: choose L/D and clearance, oil, assume temperature, S, charts, h₀ and ΔT, iterate on clearance
Compare starting friction, noise, maintenance, radial space and cost
Rolling bearings suit small motors: low starting torque, quiet enough, sealed for life
Journal bearings suit very large or very high-speed machines where life in hours is unreachable for rolling elements
State a clear recommendation with reasons

bank.q: Discuss the effect of radial clearance c and length-to-diameter ratio L/D on the performance of a hydrodynamic journal bearing. How would you choose both for a steady load at moderate speed?
outline: S carries (r/c)², so clearance changes S strongly and shifts the whole operating point
Small clearance: high load capacity but high friction and temperature, tighter tolerances needed
Large clearance: more oil flow and cooler running, but lower capacity and possible whirl
L/D near 1 is the usual compromise; low L/D leaks oil and loses pressure, high L/D overheats and misaligns
Use the Raimondi and Boyd charts at several L/D to compare h₀, friction and ΔT
Check h₀ against roughness, and temperature against oil life
Recommend a clearance range from standard tables and confirm by the temperature-rise check

bank.q: Design a full hydrodynamic journal bearing for a steady load of 20 kN at 1000 rpm: choose the oil and L/D, compute the Sommerfeld number, use the charts to fix clearance and check film thickness and temperature rise. State all assumptions.
outline: Choose L/D near 1 and a trial diameter from the allowable bearing pressure
Pick an oil grade and estimate its viscosity at the expected oil temperature
Select clearance from standard practice for that diameter
Compute P, then S
Read ε, h₀, friction variable and flow from the charts for the chosen L/D
Heat balance: friction power equals the heat carried by the oil flow plus that lost to the surroundings; find ΔT
Iterate the assumed temperature until it matches the computed one
Check h₀ against combined roughness for full film; state assumptions and safety margins

glossary.def: A machine element that supports a moving part, carries its load and reduces friction between the moving and fixed surfaces.
The replaceable ring of bearing metal in which a journal turns or slides.
A soft white-metal lining alloy of tin or lead with antimony and copper, used on steel shells because it conforms to the shaft and embeds dirt.
A raised ring on a shaft that bears against a thrust surface to take axial load.
The portion of a shaft that turns inside a bearing.
Half the difference between bush bore and journal diameter, the space available for the oil film when the shaft is centred.
The angle between the load direction and the line joining bush centre to shaft centre in a loaded journal bearing.
Load divided by the projected area, P = W/(L·d), used as the nominal pressure in bearing design.
A set of dimensionless design curves for full journal bearings giving eccentricity, film thickness, friction, oil flow and temperature rise against the Sommerfeld number for various L/D.
The commonest ball bearing, with raceway grooves that take radial load and either direction of axial load.
The life in millions of revolutions that a rolling bearing reaches or exceeds with 90% reliability under a stated load.
A multiplying factor applied to the L10 life when a reliability other than 90% is required; it is below 1 for higher reliability.
A multiplier on the calculated load that allows for shock, vibration and duty of the driven machine.
The property of an oil that lets it cling to and lubricate surfaces under boundary conditions, separate from viscosity.
A chemical added to oil or grease that reacts with the metal under high contact pressure to form a low-shear surface film.
A standard number for an oil's kinematic viscosity at 40 °C, such as ISO VG 32 or VG 68, used to specify lubricants.
Any substance placed between sliding or rolling surfaces to keep them apart and reduce friction and wear.
A full fluid film supplied by an external pump at pressure, used where the speed is too low to build hydrodynamic pressure.
The ratio c/r of radial clearance to journal radius; it appears squared in the Sommerfeld number.
An unstable self-excited motion of a lightly loaded high-speed journal in which the shaft centre circles inside the bush.
A hardened ball, cylindrical roller, needle or tapered roller that separates the bearing rings with rolling rather than sliding contact.
L10 in revolutions converted to running time, L = 10⁶ × L10 ÷ (60 × N) hours with N in rpm.
P₀ = X₀·F_r + Y₀·F_a, the load to compare against C₀ when the bearing is stationary or very slow.
Passages cut in the bush to distribute oil to the loaded zone; they are kept out of the load-carrying region so the film is not broken.
